utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today, we are to hear the Defence of Sredoje Lukic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our first witness is Mr. Veroljub Zivkovic, and we will have no opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll have no opening statement. I should say that the motion that you made for the witnesses to testify under 92 ter is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Subject, of course, to the requirements of the rule being met. You know what those requirements are. There is one other matter I should mention. It's Sredoje Lukic's motion for certification to appeal the decision of the 13th November, 2008, in relation to the admission of a particular exhibit. The Chamber, I am to say, will deny that motion, and a written decision will be given later today or, at the latest, tomorrow. I want also to mention, Mr. Ivetic, you're here. Mr. Alarid is not here?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. He's still traveling in the United States. He should be returning Wednesday morning, Your Honours, from the States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I just wanted to mention and to recall the Chamber's order pursuant to Rule 73 ter of the 27th of November. We allowed the Defence of Milan Lukic to call 45 witnesses within 60 hours of examination-in-chief. The reasons for the decision are set out in the Chamber's decision, and I want to say that the Chamber will hold the Defence strictly to the time framework that it has identified. I notice there is no application for protective measures from either side. Mr. Ivetic, does that mean that you have no application for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What it means is that we have not had an opportunity to go out in the field to meet with the witnesses and ask specifically of each one for protective measures. We do know about the MLD alibi witnesses, that they did require protective measures, and an application will be brought shortly for those; so there is at least a group that will have protective measures, although we suspect that group will expand in size once we have an opportunity to interview fully the witnesses who end up being on the final list to see who would want to apply for protective measures and what their basis would be for those protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are aware, of course, that normally you file a motion. It's done in court exceptionally. I've allowed the Prosecution exceptionally to make oral applications, but the normal rule I expect to apply, that's a motion, so it can be considered by the Trial Chamber with the other party being given an opportunity to comment on it, so that the protective measures for witnesses to be heard before the Christmas recess may exceptionally be made orally, but must be done so at the earliest opportunity. The measures for witnesses to be heard after the recess, they should be made at least two weeks prior to testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will try to stick to that, Your Honour, and there will be written motions. If we could be back up, Your Honour, for some clarification as to the order pursuant to Rule 73 ter, which we are working to try and comply with for the tomorrow deadline. We wanted to bring to Your Honours' attention, there are about seven witnesses on our list who are witnesses that were OTP witnesses who are being merely brought to authenticate their statements to be introduced into evidence, and there are five document custodian witnesses who are being put on the list because of the Prosecution's insistence that even requests for -- requests for assistance be authenticated by the records custodians. We would ask for at least those 12 witnesses to be -- to not count towards the 45 that we have since these are really witnesses that are being brought upon the direction of the OTP for administrative matters that really ought to be quick, and they are not really substantive witnesses going towards the flow of events to the Defence. So we'd like to bring that to the Court's attention, and we will work on trying to at least pare down the witness list and at least give groups of potential witnesses where we would call one out of five, one out of six, depending on who's available and who has the most -- the most -- best recollection of events to present the best testimony for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that the witnesses are being brought as a result of the Prosecution's insistence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. They -- they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, if I can. We have several witnesses for whom they were OTP witnesses. They were either named in this case as OTP witnesses or disclosed as OTP witnesses for the Vasiljevic case. They have sworn statements that contradict in many times family members or other OTP witnesses who did come here to testify, and we would be bringing them just to authenticate those OTP statements, which at one point in time the Prosecution even said, we don't know how --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- they're the statements of the OTP. So ... I apologise. The Prosecution said that they are not reliable, but those are OTP statements. So in essence, those that were being forced to bring live individuals to introduce statements, we could perhaps do that under a 92 bis except for the fact that the Prosecution is refusing to give us the contact information for those witnesses, but in any event, even if we were to bring perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- count towards our 45 total, because they're being brought upon the insistence of the Prosecution and not stipulating to some --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt, but no one has earphones on. The interpreters are asking you to slow down, Mr. Ivetic. Several times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologize, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You do tend to speak very fast --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- so you have to make a special effort to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this courtroom, I tend to speak even faster it seems than the smaller courtroom. So as I was saying, Your Honour, if we bring those seven former OTP witnesses and five document custodial -- custodian-type witnesses, we would ask for the Court to clarify its order or reconsider its order to not have those count towards our 45 witness total that was specified in the Rule 73 ter order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a brief comment. I don't recall ever having made such a blanket statement with respect to the reliability of OTP statements. It seems to me that if Mr. Ivetic wishes to introduce the statements of witnesses, there is a procedure for that. He's correct in saying it's 92 bis, and we'd be happy to, where appropriate, not oppose admission of certain statements with respect to 92 bis. He raises an issue with respect to the Prosecution providing the contact details of the witnesses. I'm not sure that's necessary for 92 bis because 92 bis would allow the registrar simply to go and validate or take the sworn portion of the statement, but I am mindful of that, and I am mindful that I have no ownership of witnesses. What I have tried to do to resolve this is I've -- I don't feel comfortable handing over to Milan Lukic the addresses and the phone numbers of witnesses without their consent, so I can either contact those witnesses and find out whether they do consent, or it seems to me one other way to do this is to have a neutral party, such as VWS, contact the witnesses and perhaps arrange some communication between the Defence team and the witness. I've spoken to Mr. De Witt, the head of VWS, on Friday, about his views on this, and he's going to let me know today whether he thinks it's something that VWS could appropriately undertake. So, you know, I will report back to the Chamber when Mr. De Witt let's me know what his views are on it, but it seems to me, that would be one way to deal with this matter. I would provide the contact information to VWS and leave it to them to, in a way that is mindful of the wishes and the security of the witnesses, to place them -- place the Defence team in communication with those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are these witnesses in respect of whom protective measures have been applied?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure all of them. I think some of them may have had some protective measures at some point, Your Honour. I would have to check that before I could speak specifically to that, but again, I'm not comfortable simply handing over the contact details. Of course, if the Chamber orders me, to I'll certainly comply with that order; but it seemed to me the more appropriate way to do this would be to have a neutral party contact those witnesses and make some arrangements, either through a conference call that they could arrange between Defence counsel and the witness if the Defence counsel want to speak to these people directly, or they could simply ask the witness, are they happy to have their contact information provided to the Defence? But it seemed to me by placing that in a neutral party, it would avoid any kind of concern they may be asked in a leading way whether or not they wanted to speak with Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please stand. I'm not going to rule on your request that -- is it 12 witnesses? 12 witnesses not be counted, in the number -- among the 45 witnesses that the Chamber has indicated the Defence will be allowed to call. I'm not going to rule on that now. I will consider it. You must file a motion, a written motion, and file that motion today. Similarly, I advise you also to file a motion requesting that the Trial Chamber consider requiring the Prosecutor to provide the contact details of the witnesses in question. That will give the Chamber some time to consider it. I can see arguments going both ways, and so I don't wish to rule on that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just maybe one additional matter to maybe relieve Mr. Ivetic of some of his burden. He said that the Prosecution was opposing any -- requiring people to come and authenticate requests for assistance. I will state on the record that the Prosecution will accept any request of assistance made to a government. So if any government in response to a request for assistance by the Milan Lukic team receives documents through an official request for assistance, I will accept that. Similarly, just as we have put forward in written filing a request for assistance for some records that we received, and the Chamber did admit them, I would expect the same treatment for the Prosecution. So if the request for assistance is from a government and officially provided by that government, the Prosecution will accept those documents as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Cepic. Your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our first witness is Mr. Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please give us your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of May, 1961, in Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I'm going to ask you to pass the document to the witness. In the meantime, could we have on our screens 65 ter Exhibit number 17. ID number is in B/C/S, 2D04-0121, and in English, 2D04-0125.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivkovic, do you see the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, I'll ask you, have you given a written statement to this Defence team on the 26th of November, 2007?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, during proofing with the Defence team of Mr. Sredoje Lukic, did you ask for certain corrections to be made to the statement?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was one of these corrections related to paragraph 2 of your statement, namely the distance between your house and the house of Mr. Milojko Popadic in the settlement where you live?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you want to change?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was written there that the distance between Mr. Milojko Popadic's house and mine was 300 metres. I noticed immediately that it was perhaps a typo. In fact, the distance is 700 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4, in the third sentence in B/C/S, which is the fourth sentence in English, did you ask that after the words: "After his arrest when he came to visit his family, I saw him ..." did you ask that to be replaced with the wording: "The first time I saw him visit his family after his arrest"?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, regarding all the other questions asked of you when you gave that statement, if I asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I tender this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 2D41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could I ask for Exhibit 65 ter number 32. ID number is 2D05-0270 in B/C/S, and in English, 2D05-2071. I'm sorry. We have corrections for the version in English language, so according to the notification from 20th of November, it is 2D05-0293. Just translation. It is official translation from the service of ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivkovic, can you see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a certificate issued by our priest, Petar Paraklis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does it confirm? What does it certify?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It certifies that it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I kindly ask admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a celebration for the village of Krtinska.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's 2D42, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have in e-court system 65 ter number 13. It's the wrong exhibit. Defence exhibit 65 ter 13, ID number 2D03-0374 and 0375. I do have this document in hard copy. It was in our package in accordance with Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivkovic, what is this document on our screens?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It's our church calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For which month, for which year?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about the year?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the year. Oh, right. Right. It's 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the St. Trinity holidays? On what dates did they fall?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: St. Trinity changes dates but is always on Sunday. Which month do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sunday the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we kindly ask for admission of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the -- what is the date that we are to look at here? Because it's not translated. What are you bringing to our attention in this church diary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the translation is now on the screen. Ah, yes. I see it. I still want you to tell us, though, what is it that you're bringing to our attention, now that we have it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we should pay attention here to the month of June, 14th June, a Sunday. It's a celebration of my -- celebrated in my village where I live, Holy Trinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Scroll down in English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I see it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And also, if I may add, this exhibit was in Mitar Vasiljevic case. It was admitted as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you wish to have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I forgot to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 2D43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivkovic. My name is Dermot Groome, and I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution, okay? I first want to ask you about your relationship with Sredoje Lukic. Would it be fair to say that you know him for approximately 20 years?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you consider yourself a good friend of Sredoje Lukic's?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: We were acquaintances. We were not dear friends. My best friends live where I live, and I see them every day, but I was good a good acquaintance with him. We were sound acquaintances, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, during the war, you and Sredoje Lukic lived quite close to each other. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic lived in that village of Krtinska, relatively close. I don't know what you mean by the word "close."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, how far did he live from your home?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 1 and a half kilometers while he used to live in the centre of the village, 1 and a half kilometers, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, do you recall having -- or giving an interview to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, Phillip Caine, about your testimony here today? Do you recall having such an interview?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during that interview, you stated that after the war began, Sredoje Lukic would come from Visegrad to visit his family in Obrenovac, and you also described that he would bring you things from Visegrad. Let me read a portion of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for counsel, I'll be referring to the English translation of the statement when I give the transcript references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we gave -- actually, we found many errors, even in B/C/S translation, and I never found that Sredoje Lukic brought the things to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm about to read the actual passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And counsel can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this is on page 21 of that transcript, line 4, and it says: "Many times he," referring to Sredoje Lukic, "helped us out too." So my question to you is, how was it that Sredoje Lukic helped you out during the war?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic did not help me out during the war, and this is not my statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you don't recall saying that to Phillip Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. As far as you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have couple versions of that transcript in English, in B/C/S, so could my learned friend Mr. Groome clarify us from which precisely transcript is page 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's what I told Mr. Cepic before Court and what I've said here in court. There are various translations, and it appears, Your Honour, that the translator that attended the interview was quite poor, made a number of errors that Mr. Cepic has pointed out. So what I'm using is the English translation of the original B/C/S under the view that's what's most important is what question was put -- did the witness hear, and what was the witness's response? So what I'm referring to when I give transcript references, it's the English translation of the B/C/S that was spoken during the course of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, Mr. Groome, if you were to read from the translation what was said just before the disputed passage and what comes after. Maybe we might have a fuller context. Mr. Cepic, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With your leave, just if we can have from which transcript is -- was 21st page which Mr. Groome quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, it's the English translation of the B/C/S. It's not the merged translation that has the -- what we now know to be incorrect translations made during the course of the interview. It is simply the English translation of the B/C/S, and it bears the number T001-1686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I was suggesting, Mr. Groome, is that perhaps the witness might have a better recollection of what you put to him, if you reminded him of what went immediately before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll read the entire passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, Mr. Caine asked you the following question: "How do you know that he," referring to Sredoje Lukic, "was coming to visit his family?" And your response was: "Well, because we have time to visit each others, usually on Saturdays and Sundays over the weekend. He was coming usually at that time, and whatever I was doing, something with the car, with the truck, I have only the weekend, since I usually say," and there's a word that was not caught on tape, "since I usually say to find a job. That I do that. Let's say in the afternoons and over the weekend and so. And my house is also on the way. It is in view. It has always been like that, always. Many times he helped us out too. I would give him something, I do not know, some part and so." So again, sir, my question is, do you remember giving that answer to Mr. Phillip Caine? Do you recall giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say what you just read out, but I did not say that he brought things. This is an obvious mistake. I have my own tape while I was giving this statement, and I know that it can be translated in detail what -- the first thing you said, it was not true, but the latter statement that you read out was correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So where I read: "Many times he helped us out too." Again, what was the help that Sredoje Lukic gave you and your family, or you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: While working at Milojko Popadic's, while I was repairing his trucks, and when he would come over the weekend when he was free, Sredoje used to help us out with those trucks. I would give him a part to sandpaper and prepare for installation. In this context, it was that I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that the Chamber is clear, you are a car mechanic in that you fix the locks of cars and you fix the body of cars, and it is your testimony that Sredoje Lukic helped you out during this period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a locksmith by trade, but I've been dealing with car body mechanics, painting of cars. I do everything except the mechanical parts. I can deal with everything else concerning cars and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's what Sredoje Lukic helped you out with, that type of work, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When he would come to Mr. Popadic where I was usually working on trucks over weekends, when Sredoje used to come, he would help out, not always, not regularly, but when he happened to be at Mr. Popadic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just in the interest of time, if I could ask you to answer my question with a simple yes or no if possible, I'd appreciate that. Did you attend Sredoje Lukic's wedding?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to clarify the following portion from the transcript. This is page 23 beginning at line 11: "Why I think he worked in Visegrad first, it is because when he got married to Milojko's sister, when they invited me to celebrate it, then they said that he was a policeman and that he worked in Visegrad." Can you explain what you meant when you said that in your interview to Mr. Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he married -- he married most probably at Visegrad, but first time I visited Milojko Popadic's after his marriage, when he came to that place, I was there working on trucks. This is how we met. But I did not attend his wedding at Visegrad. I've never been to Visegrad in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, what height is Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic is around 180 centimetres, give or take a couple of centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was his age, approximate age, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the year he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your best estimate. Your best estimate.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: 25, 26 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean, when I met him how old he was? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In 1992, the period of time that you've come to testify about, that's the time, the age at that time.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, 25, 26 years or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would have been his approximate weight at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 90, 90 kilogrammes. We are similar, approximately, in stature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you ever remember him going unshaven around that time period?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: There were times when he had some leisure time, he did not have any duties. When he was off-duty, he would grow a couple of days' beard, but of course when he went back to work, he had to be clean-shaven because that comes with the job. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when he had not shaved for a couple of days, would that be something that would be clearly visible?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What could be visible? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you is, some people have a light beard, some people have a heavy beard. When he didn't shave for a couple of days, was it something that was readily seen by people who would see him?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It could be noticed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there's a witness scheduled to testify here by the name of Milojko Popadic. What is your relationship to Mr. Popadic?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a good friend with Milojko Popadic. We've been working together for years, and we grew to be friends over that time, following from all the jobs that I did for him at his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Popadic owns a trucking firm and he regularly gave you work during this period in the repair of his trucks?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 90 per cent of cases, I repaired his trucks, and I still do that when the need arises. Whenever there is a job to be done on a truck, I do it, when he works at construction house or something gets bent or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you also related to him by marriage?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we're no relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's not your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's also another witness by the name of Branko Bugarski. Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I do know Branko Bugarski. We're not friends that would visit each other, but I know of him, and he lives in the same community of Krtinska where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And have you also done work for his son, Darko?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He bought him a truck, and then we overhauled the whole truck, of course, except the mechanics, but the body, the locks, paint, everything except the mechanics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the war -- I see from your interview with Mr. Caine that you told him that during the war Sredoje Lukic first came to live with Milojko Popadic and then moved to an apartment that Milojko found in the centre of Krtinska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who owned the apartment that Milojko found for Sredoje Lukic to live in?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Bugarski from Krtinska was the owner. His mother used to live there. Then it was empty, vacant, and he rented it out to Mr. Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to you, on the Day of Holy Trinity in 1992, Sredoje Lukic was living in the apartment owned by Bugarski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know if he was paying rent?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, neither did I ask him nor did I have a need to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the following exhibit be called up on e-court. It's 0635-2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during -- while that's being called up, during the course of your interview with Mr. Caine, did he ask you to make some marks on a map of Krtinska to indicate where different people lived, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He showed me a map, but it is not an original map of that village. It would have been much easier if it were an original. It is a tourist map, but I can find my bearings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It's being loaded now, and while we're working with this map, I would ask if we could prepare for e-court the e-court exhibit named Mlad. It's a large photograph. It may take a while to upload. So sir, while we're looking at that map there, is that the map that you made markings on during the interview with Mr. Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to change in this map? Is it still accurate?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It's approximately accurate, but not all the roads and paths are indicated here. There are many more roads and paths than are shown on this map, but I orientate myself by this main road, and this is -- I indicated in relation to that main road where each house is. If I had a precise map of Krtinska, I could show you all the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I think I may be able to assist you with that. So based upon your testimony that this is the map that you marked during your interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I would now tender into evidence, Your Honour, ERN 0635-2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the document Mlad be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is an aerial photograph of the Krtinska village. I'd ask you to take a look at it and ask you, do you recognize it? Are you able to get your bearings from this aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the thermo electrical or power plant is. This is my main reference point. If I were to know where it is in relation to this section, I could tell you where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and if my learned friend has got a bigger map, and this is map is misleading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's simply a picture -- I'm not sure how it could be misleading. It's a photograph taken from the air. I can assist the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying it's not accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is just part, one part of that suburb. It's not the whole area. This is just part -- this is Mlad. It's not the whole Krtinska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see whether the witness can help us with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if it helps orient you, the power station would be on the road going to the right of the map. Does that assist you? You will be able to make marks on this map, but I just want to see if you're able to orient yourself on this map.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It really is not very clear, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If he's not able to identify where it is, Your Honour, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during your interview with Phillip Caine, you indicated that you knew Sredoje Lukic worked in Belgrade for a period of time, but you were uncertain about when. What is your memory, best memory, with respect to when Sredoje Lukic worked in Belgrade? In the interview, you thought it might have been 1987, 1988, or 1989. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately from 1988, 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Cepic was on his feet, but he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is late on better translation in B/C/S. They started something wrongly and later on it is proper. Thank you. I apologize for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. Please give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it was in 1988, 1989. I stated that I'm not 100 per cent certain, but approximately that would be it, that period when Sredoje Lukic used to work in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for how long a period is it your belief he worked in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: For a brief period, he worked there, but I don't know whether one or two years. A brief period. I remember that by the fact that he would visit Milojko more frequently because that's closer to where he lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that you're not sure, it was either in 1988 or 1989. Do you recall in your interview with Mr. Caine you also said that it might also be 1987?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, during that period I think it was around 1988, 1988. I reiterate, I cannot tell you precisely the year, the date. What I do not know, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, but your memory with respect to dates is quite important in your evidence. You recognize that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. But I cannot give you a precise date when he worked in Belgrade. He was a policeman in Belgrade. What I do know is that he used to frequent Milojko's place more frequently because he lived closer by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could read you a portion of your statement or your interview with Mr. Caine, and if you could tell me whether it's correct, and it's at page 19 beginning on line 20. "If my memory is good, he worked in Belgrade for one period, sometime in 1987, 1988, 1989. I do not know exactly which period. I cannot assert that." Do you recall saying that to Mr. Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've had numerous cases before the courts of Serbia, some having to do with violations of traffic laws, and others having to do with violations of the law of public order and peace and other violations of the Criminal Code. In order to save time, I've prepared a table from the information we have received from the government of Serbia. I'm going to ask that it be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is document ZIV-CONV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at this table and examine it, and tell us whether it accurately summarizes the numerous cases you have had brought against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask, to give the witness the benefit of seeing the entire document if it's possible, perhaps we could just look at the B/C/S at this stage, and then if he recognizes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, could I ask you just to read over that, and my question to you is, does it accurately summarize the cases that you have had before the courts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about these documents. I had traffic violations. I know that, and I know of another case when there was a traffic jam -- sorry, there was a commotion. My uncle had come, and I arrived then and pulled my uncle out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you some specific questions about one of the cases here. I'm just asking you -- there's three pages to this document. Let me please ask the usher to advance to the second page. If you would look at that, and all I'm asking you is whether the information on this -- again, it's a table created from information received from the government of Serbia, if it appears accurate to you, to be an accurate record of the cases you've had before the courts of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But did he address the first page? Did he speak to the accuracy of the first page? You have moved to the second now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was going to give him an opportunity to see the entire document, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Proceed. But let us hear Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do not object to this document, but most of this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Cepic please speak into the microphone. Mr. Cepic is inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone. They can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologize. I apologize. Your Honour, I do not object informations, but related to most of these procedures, this witness is acquitted, according to this document, so I don't see the purpose to discuss about some cases where he's acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just an accurate reflection of the cases. I'm certainly not going to question him on anything other than a conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you be shown the last page. I'm sorry. There's very little on the last page. But sir, do you recognize these is being accurate descriptions of cases that you had before the courts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The table is a summary of information we received from the government of Serbia regarding cases that you had that were brought against you in the courts of Serbia, so my question to you is, looking at that table, and we can go back to any page that you want to take another look at, does it accurately reflect -- does it agree with your memory of the cases you had before the courts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember in the last ten years that I have ever appeared in court. Maybe if you told me again about some of these cases, I would remember, but maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's maybe go back to the first page. Let me ask you about number 3 on the first page. Now, on the 13th of April, 2001, you were convicted in the municipal court of Obrenovac of paragraph 1 of Article 220 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, a code starting with the title called "Violent Behavior," and it's a very long title that describes several ways in which that crime can be committed. Do you recall being convicted of that crime in 2001, arising out of an incident that occurred in May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember vaguely. It's some sort of disgrace inflicted upon citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you specific questions about it, do you admit that you were convicted of this crime, this violation of Article 220, paragraph 1? Do you admit that you were convicted of that crime?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. I remember very vaguely some sort of incident, but I don't know if I was convicted or if I was sentenced or fined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me call up the judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that my learned friend wrongly quoted the paragraph of this article, and also, as I said, we do not object the procedures against this client, but what is the source of -- this table, is it made by OTP or from the government of Republic of Serbia which we have on our screens now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As I stated, Your Honour, it is a table made of information provided by the government of Serbia. I do actually have the computer printout from the government detailing all of these cases. It's a little bit hard to read, but I'm certainly happy to call that up and tender that as a companion to this table if Mr. -- and I see Mr. Cepic is agreeing with that procedure. So it'll take me a minute to get that released. It wasn't released before. Then I'll call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But for now, could I call up the actual judgement against you, and that is 0645-2787, 0645-2801. While that's being called up, sir, is it your testimony that you do not recall being convicted of a criminal offense seven years ago?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had these traffic violations, and if I had any more serious offenses than that, I would need to be reminded. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, this is an incident that arose and you were accused of driving your car into a fence that was put up by a neighbor of yours. There was some dispute over the fence, that you drove your car knocking down the fence and then assaulted at least one person. Do you recall that? It occurred on the 20th of May, 2000?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that when I grazed that fence, that man hit me, and then a commotion ensued. I cannot remember all the details, but I remember grazing that fence. Then that man started chasing me, and then we had a clash. That's what I remember, but not the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You recognize that you've been convicted of assaulting that person and knocking down that fence in the municipal court of Obrenovac, do you not?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if this is a document from our courts, I accept it. It's probably true that I was convicted if it says so in the document. If it's a document from our authorities, I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then when the case was appealed to the appellate court, the second-instance court actually increased your sentence to a 6-month sentence. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender the document that's on the screen, 0645-2787, 0645-2801. It's the first instance judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is admitted as Exhibit P199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, was the other person who was involved in the altercation also charged? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, reading the judgement, it does not seem so, but I did not ask for the record of the other person, but there are certain statements made in this document before you that I think it makes clearing that the judges in this case rejected that theory put forward by Mr. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, do you accept responsibility for the crime that you were convicted for?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply don't remember. I cannot tell you honestly very precisely. I remember something happened, but whether I was convicted, how I was sentenced, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I would call up 0645-2690, 0645-2691. This is the criminal history printout, and I think Mr. Cepic will have more familiarity than all of us with reading such computer printouts. And if Mr. Cepic has no objection, then I will be tendering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is not. If we're speaking about the previous document, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, it's not the previous document. It's not on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we see it, and later on I can raise maybe objection, maybe no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the previous document which we've seen on our screens -- I'm sorry, which we have seen on our screens is not a criminal record from our country. It doesn't look like any criminal record from Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record's clear, what's on the screen now is what has just been introduced in evidence, and it's the actual judgement. Now what's appearing on the screen is the computer printout of the record of convictions in the original. And if Mr. Cepic has no objection, I would tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No objection. This is -- I think that is authentic document from my country, but it is a different procedure than the criminal procedure, this record of verdicts or whatever is from completely different procedure than is the criminal procedure, but no objections. It is authentic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What are you saying? It's not a criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what kind of procedure was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We call that [Interpretation] misdemeanor procedure. [In English] Misdemeanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is -- if I may add some clarification, just for traffic fines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand. I understand the difference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear, what Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My colleagues are wondering what the point is of this cross-examination. The substance of this witness's evidence is that the 14th of June was Pentecost. Now, you're cross-examining him about his record, whether misdemeanor or criminal, and of course that is entirely proper in certain cases. It goes to credibility. But it's either the 14th of June is Pentecost or not. His credibility as that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would take a very different view. It's not whether the 14th is really Pentecost, and I would probably concede that according to the church calendar it seems that it is. What's really is important is whether this witness can be believed when he says that on that day he was having a beer with Sredoje Lukic when it is alleged by the Prosecution that he was some distance away perpetrating a crime in Visegrad. So his credibility is important, and I believe with the next few questions it will be even clearer why, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you did say that, just a few minutes ago, that you grazed the fence, so it seems that you admit that you did drive your car into a fence. You admit that, do you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there was a bend, and that's where I grazed that fence. I cannot be quite sure now how serious it was and what exactly it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it also true that -- well, did you knock down some of the poles on the fence?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I did. As far as I remember, I did. That's how it started, but I can't remember every detail very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the fence that you knocked down was a fence that you -- there was a dispute regarding that fence. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you admit that you struck someone during this exchange, that you hit someone?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I struck anyone. There was a push -- a lot of pushing and shoving, but whether I really hit someone, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you accept the possibility that you may have hit someone?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. That man whose fence I grazed, he was more aggressive. He was violent. He started that fight. I cannot remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, was he also charged with a misdemeanor or any other offense, Witness? I'm asking whether the other man was also charged with a misdemeanor or some other offense, or were you the only one who was charged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't remember at all whether he was charged because when you have a fight with someone over something, it's quite normal that you are not on good terms after that, so I couldn't come up to him and ask him if he was charged or convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 0645-2701, 0645-2704 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking that what be brought to the screen now is the record of interview that the -- the questions that the judge asked you and the recording of your answers. Do you recall being questioned by a judge with respect to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't see any relevance for this case. There is a judgement -- we did not object about the judgement, but we -- if we open now, that case, I think that is not subject for cross-examination here before this high-ranking Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It goes to credibility. I think this is what Mr. Groome is saying, whether the witness is credible. So let us see where Mr. Groome is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the bottom of page 3 in the English translation. And I apologize, I'm not exactly sure where in the B/C/S. I'm trying to get that information now. It's also at the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've admitted here today at least to the possibility that you struck someone, and you do admit that you did knock down some of that fence. So I want to read you a portion of the statement that you gave to the judge in this case. "So it is not true that I hit Branislav or Petar with my fist, and it is also not true that on that day I broke down several poles of the fence by car." So my question to you now is whether you now admit that the statement that you originally made to the investigating judge was false.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It can't be false. I can't have given a false statement before a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But here in court, you admit to knocking down at least the fence, and here in the statement that you gave to the judge, you deny knocking down the fence. So which is the truth and which is not?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: What's true is probably that he was claiming that I had deliberately knocked down the fence, and there was nothing deliberate in what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember saying to the judge in this case that you denied knocking down -- or I could quote again: "It is also not true that on that day I broke down several poles of the fence by car."

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. You have to believe me. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 0645-2701, the record of interview, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the appeals judgement, the second instance judgement be called up. It's 0645-2787, 0645-2801.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in this judgement, there are certain findings made with respect to some of your -- with respect to your character and some of your propensities. While it's being called up, on page 4 of the judgement, it states: "It is a common knowledge that accused Dragoljub and Veroljub," that being you, the second one, "are in bad relation themselves. It is a common knowledge that the accused Dragoljub used to beat up his parents and that the accused Veroljub still does the same." Were the judges correct when they made a finding that you, in the past, had beaten up your parents?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It's a blatant lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Similarly, on page 4 of the judgement, the judges credit the evidence provided by a person by the name of Jelena Novakovic, that: "The accused Veroljub beat up his wife approximately 16 years ago when she was 8 months pregnant. Both accused have the reputation of having a tendency to fight and argue."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm going to raise now objection as I heard many times from OTP. My learned friend Mr. Groome now quotes testimony of other witnesses in that procedure. That was in previous situation, now, again, related to that lady, which name is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak in the mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He's just quoting allegations of witness. And as I understood, Mr. Groome now would like to raise the issue of character, which is not the issue of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think character has an awful lot to the with credibility, and I think someone -- court were to find that someone beat their 8-month-pregnant wife it's something that the Chamber would be entitled to consider with respect to credibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true. And, Your Honour, may I just say something. This person, Jelena, who gave that statement, that's the daughter of the person whose fence I grazed. Her husband was director, Mr. Markovic, and our courts at that time were so corrupt that the powerful people who could pull the strings in a little town like ours could swing the judgement in their favor. Everyone knows, who lives in our parts, how things were at that time. In my country, I admit that we had those wars. We had inflation. We had a lot of corruption, and we still have some, although to a lesser degree, but it's really horrific. I can spend months telling you about that. I have had no incident less serious than this one, but that's how it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir, I would not allow the objection raised by Mr. Cepic because character is an aspect of credibility, but, Mr. Groome, it seems to us that you have dealt with this issue sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's my last question. If I just could summarize what I believe the witness's position, and then I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So sir, it seems that what you're saying is that you deny responsibility despite being convicted for this crime, and you assert that you were convicted wrongly of this crime because the courts in Obrenovac are corrupt, even in the year 2002. Is that a correct statement of your position?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time and even now, the courts are quite corrupt, especially when dealing with people in power who have money, because it's a small town where I live, Obrenovac. Everybody knows everyone. Many, many things were in play here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your position that you were wrongfully convicted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because I told you how it started. It was a most trivial incident that grew into a whole mountain by the end it was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this time I would tender 0645-2787, that's the second instance judgement against Mr. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to move to the Feast of the Holy Trinity. You stated in your interview with Mr. Caine that 90 per cent [Realtime transcript read in error "October"] of the people celebrate the Feast of the Holy Trinity in the village because it is the patron saint of the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the religious holiday of our village, Pentecost.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologize. I think that we have a wrong word in the transcript, page 38, line 3, "90 October," but I think that Mr. Groome did not mention October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the date you gave, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I've given a date. I think I just said Holy Trinity, Feast of Holy Trinity. I'm sorry. I said 90 per cent of people. That's the number I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question to you, Mr. Zivkovic, is, is it true that 90 per cent of the people in your village celebrate the Feast of Holy Trinity because it is the patron saint of the village, it's a village feast day? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I get too far, I neglected to formally tender the criminal history printout, the court document that Mr. Cepic recognized as 0645-2690, 0645-2691, and I would tender that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If it is a table which is made by OTP, I object. If it's just the document issued by government of Serbia, we do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the same information. It can be checked -- I mean, there's nothing added. It's just placed in a way that I think is more accessible to Your Honours. Can Mr. Cepic please state specifically upon what basis he finds that that table's objectionable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the printout?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, there's the printout, Your Honour, that's a computer printout that's somewhat cryptic. The table organises it into about five columns and includes the information from the printout. Again, I don't understand what the -- why it would be objectionable to make it a little bit more organised and more easily read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not a printout. It is a document which is made probably by the source of government of Serbia. I cannot say that, but it is a document, as far as I remember, it is a table which is made by OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might summarize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is made by OTP, but it is -- are you saying it doesn't accurately reflect -- Mr. Cepic, I am asking you. Are you saying it doesn't accurately reflect what was in the government document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not object related to the judgement, and we already have admitted the judgement in the system, but other procedures are acquitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If there are acquittals there, then we will see that, but Mr. Groome was referring to a charge that led to a conviction. Are you saying that that is not so? The witness hasn't really denied it. He has said that he was wrongly convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, the point is, we did not object the content, but the source is a problem because that table made OTP, we haven't got official letter from government of Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, there's just one additional question I wanted to ask you about the criminal conviction. I note from the criminal record papers that we were provided, I note that one month before you gave your statement in this case, an effort was made to expunge this conviction from your record. And my question to you is, what, if any, relationship in your mind exists between the attempt to expunge that conviction in October 2007 and your giving of a statement in this case in November of 2007?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think that needs to be broken down. Who made the attempt to have it expunged?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's simply an item in the printout, Your Honour, saying that there was an expungement in October of 2007, and I'm just inquiring from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think first you should find out from him if he knows anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in October of 2007 there is an entry on your record indicating an expungement of the criminal conviction that we are now discussing?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I do know, in accordance with our laws, three years after your sentence expires, you receive a letter that something is erased or expunged. Moreover, I heard that this was done automatically pursuant to the law because it is, as I understand it, considered that a sentence has been served, and it can be expunged ex officio after a certain lapse of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know, and I don't recall ever appearing in court in the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you don't recall ever receiving a letter?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I may have received. I know that it is a usual practice of our courts, after your sentence expires, three years from that date you receive a letter. It's possible I may have received such a letter, but I do not recall it as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could return to the Feast of the Holy Trinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be glad to assist my learned friends from OTP about that issue if there is any doubt exist because according to criminal law of my country, under the Article 94 or 95, it is possible in all judgements, you know, for the low-level crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome did not press the question after I suggested that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- preliminary questions need to be asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now, returning to the Holy Trinity feast, you stated in your interview that earlier that day, you assisted your wife in cooking a lunch on the morning of Trinity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I always usually do so. I help her out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is the meal that celebrates the feast day, is that a mid-day meal, a lunch?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately so, yes. It's lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to the custom, what do people eat in the evening? Do they simply eat what's left over from the mid-day meal, or do they cook another meal to celebrate Trinity in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, the leftovers from lunch. Whoever makes pot roast, there are leftovers. In my case, this was so. Whoever wanted to have some leftovers for dinner did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be your understanding that that would be the custom in the village; the similar practice would have been followed by other families in Krtinska?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: In which sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That everyone would celebrate with a large meal mid-day and in the evening simply eats whatever is -- remains.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about other households. There are people who, if they had a heavy lunch, they skip dinner, and people do not visit each other customarily on that day. Everybody celebrates it at their own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I right in thinking that the big shopping day for the preparations for the meal would be the Saturday or Friday before the Sunday?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: What shopping do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When people buy the food to prepare for the meal. Am I correct in believing that it would be done on the Saturday or the Friday before the feast day, which is on the Sunday?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: That depends on the household.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you indicated in your interview and you've just indicated now, that it is a time for family. And in your interview at page 27, beginning at line 18, you stated: "When it was lunchtime, then mainly household members were there again because, as I am saying, everyone in the village celebrates and thus it is not right to go to someone else's house, et cetera." Do you recall making that statement to Mr. Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some 90 per cent of the people in my village do so. I don't want to say 100 per cent because there may be people living there who had moved in recently and have not acquired the customs, but 90 per cent of the village do celebrate Holy Trinity as the village feast day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you also indicated in your interview that no one works on this day. Reading again from the transcript of your interview: "Well, when we woke up in the morning, it is the day when no one works in the village, so no one is doing anything. It is not good to work on that day because the village celebrates its feast." Later on that page, you say: "Absolutely no one works anything, except feed the livestock if you have any." So is it your testimony that no one works on this feast day in the village?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: For you to fully understand me, I must say this. I described the situation in my village. Whoever celebrates this do that at home, but people who work in shifts or in the state administration or in the power plant, this is not a holiday, a bank holiday, so that such people have to work; but what I meant by not working, I mean they are not working the land or anything in their -- in their yards. If they have livestock, they have to feed it. As I stated, this is not a bank holiday, a public holiday. People who work in such services have to work on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it seems that you indicated that at least the people in Krtinska who were celebrating this as their village feast day, they did not go to work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I reiterate, people who do not work in companies, if it happened that I had to work my shift, I would have come home after the shift and celebrated Holy Trinity. Other people usually rest on weekends, and the Holy Trinity always falls on a weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's time for the break. How much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's hard to approximate, Your Honour, but there are still a fair few questions that I wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the question of time for cross-examination will arise. The court deputy will inform me how long you have been, and we'll decide how much longer you -- oh, you have taken 50 minutes. Another 15 minutes, another 15, 20 minutes. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness isn't in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have some preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to be brief, Your Honour, because it relates to our ability to bring witnesses for this week. I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Cepic's case when it started and we had advised court staff of this. Your Honour, I have to report that the two witnesses we had scheduled for this week cannot attend due to scheduling of other obligations. We of course will work on trying to obtain witnesses for the following week but have no possibility of obtaining any visas for any new witnesses to come to replace them for this week. There was a -- that was one of the logistical considerations why we had requested more time previously, that the witnesses are in the region and they cannot just fax, e-mail or send copies of passports which are needed for the visa procedure. We need to send someone on the terrain to go to Serbia, to Bosnia to pick those up. We had asked the registry to approve our case manager as an investigator for those purposes, and that request was denied. We are now working on trying to get another person authorized for that. The phone ban that was in effect in the last week prevented counsel from going out into the field because the only communications the client had were with the privileged line number here in the Hague, and we were therefore in the gaol every day and dealing with that situation last week. That could not let us -- could not let us go out into the field. We do have to report that there was adverse media coverage that is still being felt out in the field. In that regard, we may have to do a filing to try and get some of that straightened out, but we are bringing that to the attention, and as a corollary to that, it is anticipated that the Sredoje Lukic case will likely conclude sometime by Wednesday.
