If that is the case, we would ask to postpone our opening statement until the Thursday, because as I'd indicated Mr. Alarid will be returning that Wednesday morning and would like to have an opportunity to get his feet under him and prepare a concise and proper opening in that regard. And that way, since we would not have any ability to present witnesses, we would not be using up more of the time that we would have allocated for the case for this week, Your Honours. And that's all I have at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not a good start, because the two witnesses who are scheduled to testify on the behalf of Mr. Lukic you say can't attend because of scheduling conflicts with other obligations, but when did you find that out? I mean, isn't that something that should have been discovered?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had spoken with one of the gentlemen on Friday, and we have not yet heard back from the second individual, so that was when I had personally found out about it when contacting them via telephone to -- this gentleman lives in, I believe, in Austria is where I contacted him at the time, and that's when we came up with that information. That's why I brought it to the Court's attention at the first available opportunity, as I believe it is my obligation to do. And again, the situation was hampered by the inability to go out into the field this past week because we were dealing with the matters that have now been resolved as to the ban on Mr. Lukic's communications with the field that was initiated upon the Office of the Prosecutor. Without going into the details of that, I think we know the parameters of that and we'll probably be doing a filing with respect to that, but it's unfortunate that the timing was such that it really prevented any work on that aspect being done upon the filing of the 65 per list that was filed just, I think, a day after the ban was asked for by the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see how we get on, and we'll deal with your problems when we reach your case. But what I understand you to be saying is that Mr. Alarid would be in a position to make his opening statement on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe the usher has gone to get the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I am limited in the time that I have to ask you questions, so I'm going to ask you, wherever possible, to answer yes or no. I ask you to excuse me if I interrupt you, and know that Mr. Cepic will have some additional time that he can ask you questions if he feels some information has been -- should come out, okay? So I'd ask for your cooperation in that regard. Sir, you also said in your interview with Mr. Caine that during the period of great inflation that took over the former Yugoslavia that the store that is the subject of your testimony had practically nothing on its shelves. Do you remember saying that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that when inflation started, not immediately but a bit later, two or three years later, this store was closed. Now we have a different privately owned store, and the one that I discussed used to be publicly owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me read from your interview, and you tell me whether you said this. This is at page 32, line 27: "No, the store does not operate anymore. It does not operate for a long time. When there was inflation, from the moment of the inflation on, it was operating during the inflation, and the situation was becoming worse and worse, so that the shelves were practically empty." Do you remember saying that to Mr. Caine? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but later. Inflation was not felt immediately, but its effects were felt later, and this is how I tried to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, in doing some research after you had said that, it seems that in June of 1992, that very month, the record of inflation had been broken, and I have a newspaper article I could call up, but to save time, let me read you the headline of the newspaper article and see if you will not agree with me. It's from Borba, and the head of the article, it's dated the 1st of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologize, but I think that this witness is not expert for economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking him about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, is he being cross-examined as to suggest that expertise is required?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is trying to ask him some economic parameters from news articles, so I'm a little bit confused about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me hear the questions first, and then I'll determine whether they're questions for an expert or just somebody with ordinary common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So sir, the title of this article from the 1st of July in Borba is: "The June triple-digit inflation of 102.3 per cent ingloriously broke the record as the highest in the history of Yugoslavia." My question to you is, do you recall that in June 1992 there was an extremely high rate of inflation in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Inflation did not peak then. Hyperinflation went and stood at a couple of thousand of per cent, not just a couple of hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the witness even knows about hyperinflation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So sir, is it your evidence that this grocery store owner had his shop open on a day, a holiday, in which you have said that most people in the village did not work, that everyone was home with their families, that people had their main meal of the day at lunchtime, and that in the evening many people ate leftovers, and that if we accept that there was inflation during this period, there may have been very little on his shelves to sell. Is it still your testimony that that shop was open on the Feast of the Holy Trinity in 1992? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me several questions. I cannot answer whether yes or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question simply is, was -- given all the factors that I have mentioned to you, is it your evidence that that shop was open on the 14th of June, 1992, the Feast of the Holy Trinity, which was celebrated in Krtinska as the village feast day? Was the shop open or closed that day?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that while the argument you described may have taken place at some point in time, that it was impossible for it to have taken place on the 14th of June because I believe that grocery store was not open. How do you respond to my assertion to you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I state that the store was open and that that incident took place on that day. My memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If your memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, in the transcript at 50, line 8, your question was: "Was the shop open or closed that day?" And the answer is yes. We need to know, what is he answering affirmatively to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it correct that your evidence is that that shop was open on that day? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to read you a portion of your interview and ask you whether it is accurate. The portion is from page 30, beginning at line 6, and it was in response to a question from Phil Caine regarding how you were so certain it was 1992. You said: "Well, I know because it was -- because it was the first. It was the first. I remember because of the war, when the war broke out. So after the war, it was maybe two months after the war. It was the first post-war Trinity, in fact, in the beginning of the war." Is this the information that you provided Mr. Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the first Holy Trinity after the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you are certain that this event took place on the first June 14th, approximately two months after the start of the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this happened on the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you mark this day by its relationship to the start of the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the break-out of the war it happened, this is the first Holy Trinity. Everybody remembered that day because the war had broken out not a long time ago prior to that, and this was the first Holy Trinity that we celebrated after the breakout of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, many people would agree that the war began with the conflict that occurred in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991, when Serb Croats attacked Croatian police forces, beginning a very long period of conflict. A very violent war occurred throughout the summer of 1991 and into the fall of 1991. The siege of Vukovar took place between August 1991 and November 1991, during which nearly the entire city was destroyed and thousands killed. Immediately following the fall of Vukovar was the well-publicized executions of captives in Ovcara. The war broke out in the late summer or spring of 1991. Isn't that when the war broke out, sir?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in our minds, the real war started in Bosnia. That was the most serious war. There had been a war, if you wish, in Slovenia, too but that was nothing much. We think of the real war as the one in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, you living in Belgrade did not consider the separation of Croatia from Yugoslavia and the siege of Vukovar a war?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I did not believe they would really separate. As far as I remember, the army was already deployed there, and I thought it wouldn't happen. The real war started in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the first Holy Trinity two months after the start of the war would have been in June of 1991. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was on the 14th of June, 1992, because I'm telling you, it was after the war broke out in Bosnia. We'll always remember that Pentecost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read your characterization of the argument that you witnessed between Sredoje Lukic and the shopkeeper. This is page 42, beginning at line 17. Mr. Caine asked you: "When it came to the verbal conflict or whatever, was it something strong, was there screaming a bit, or was it --" And then you say: "Well, it was not. It was a little argument about empties, something like, Milojko will return it to you. Do you not know me. Well, Vesko will confirm that I am Milojko's guest, and so. The salesman was really a little bit crueler as a salesman. I mean, take me for example. If I was a salesman and I know an inhabitant having guests, I would tolerate that, but it was nothing serious. They were just verbally ..." And then you finish your answer. Am I correct in understanding that it was really a very minor incident, this dispute that Sredoje Lukic had with the store owner about the deposits on a crate of beer bottles, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was more like persuasion, Why aren't you letting me do this, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after this happened, there was no real reason to ever discuss this again between you and Sredoje Lukic, was there?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When we got out, we continued that talk. We did discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But after that night was behind you, in the 15 years that have elapsed, up until the time Mr. Cepic asked you about this, had you ever discussed this dispute with Sredoje Lukic again?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember whether I talked about it with him, but with my own friends, whenever we celebrated the Pentecost for the next two or three years, we remembered it. On that day, there is usually no incidents. Everybody is in a good mood and everybody's getting along well, and that day was memorable because of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that in the years since then, you have talked about it with people who weren't there about this short verbal dispute about a deposit over empty beer bottles. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that with the friends with whom I had been standing together then, the friends I usually meet at those celebrations, I discussed it later, over the next two or three years. I can't talk about the incident with someone who did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to change the topic now. You know that Sredoje Lukic was held by some Muslims at the dam in Visegrad. He was held captive. You know about that event, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw it in the evening news bulletin on Radio Television Serbia. They showed it in the prime-time news bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you saw the news bulletin, it actually showed Sredoje Lukic after he was released from captivity, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I saw it on the news, just that they had been arrested. It was a brief piece of news.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a news item and see if you recognize this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that V000-1286 be played, and we'll be playing it on the Sanction system, control from the Prosecutor's desk. Your Honour, we were unable to synchronize the transcript, so I have hard copies here. I'd ask that they be passed out before we play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, there'll be a film played on one of the screens before you, I believe the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who's back is that that we saw just before this man here?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see properly. I didn't see the face. Will you rewind it so I can look more carefully?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They wanted to slaughter us."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry. We're rewinding it now. Did you see Sredoje Lukic on this tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this not the back of Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the back of Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your interview with Mr. Caine, you said that there were scars from where cigarettes had been put out on his back. Are we able to see those scars here?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they can be seen here. I can't see on this screen, but I know that Sredoje Lukic had told me he had been mistreated, beaten, they had shaved their hair, extinguished cigarettes on their skin. I don't know about this extinguishing of cigarettes, whether they did it only to him or to everyone. That's the story he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But he told you that they put out cigarettes on his skin.

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He said in the plural, Up there when they had arrested us, they mistreated us, they beat us, they shaved our heads, they beat us, they put out cigarettes on us. He was talking in the plural. I don't know who he was referring to specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention once again to the screen, and we'll continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that Sredoje Lukic that we're looking at there now?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: On the right is Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that exhibit V000-1286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the last few questions I have for you have to deal with how you came to be a witness in this case, and I would like to read you a portion of your interview and ask you whether it is still accurate. And this is at page 50, line -- beginning at line 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAINE ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "Can you explain to us how come that you are giving this statement?" And you state: "Well, one day he came, and a lawyer came, and this Milojko Popadic came, because when he was coming, he remembered the incident. Well, I don't know how he got in touch with Milojko, what kind of contacts they had. I don't know that, but he came that day. One day he and Milojko and the lawyer came." My question to you is, when you say "he remembered the incident," you were referring to Milojko Popadic as the one who remembered what happened on Holy Trinity in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Milojko Popadic came together with the lawyer, Mr. Djuro Cepic, to visit me. And then Milojko asked me if I remembered that incident on that Holy Trinity, and I asked him, Which Holy Trinity, there have been many. And then he recalled to me the day, the first Holy Trinity after the war and the incident with Milan Kozica in the shop, and that was it. That was my first contact with Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it was Milojko Popadic who 15 years after the event reminded you of what happened on this Holy Trinity, what you say is the first Holy Trinity after the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not that he reminded me. I remembered that incident because I remembered it was the first Holy Trinity after the war. I looked up the church calendar for that year, and I looked up the date. I know that Holy Trinity is always on a Sunday, but it can be on different dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this first conversation that you had about this event, you had it with Mr. Cepic, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And present during that interview, that first conversation you had about this, was Milojko Popadic, correct?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Milojko just asked me what I described to you a moment ago, and then Mr. Cepic took me towards his car. He had come by car, and then we talked a little while Milojko was looking at some cars. Since my job is to paint cars and repair the body of cars, he was looking at some cars in my shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to play you the actual audiotape of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's T001-1686, and it's marked as clip 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are we ready to play it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's going to be played now for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: PC: "So did you actually take Mr. Cepic to the shop to show him?" VZ: "Yes, because it was close to my place, and Mr. Cepic asked if could we go and see the shop, and I said, yes, of course, because it's very close by." PC: "Okay, and did Mr. Popadic go with you?" VZ: "Yes, he was present too." PC: "Okay. And then what -- presumably you described the events of that day when Sredoje had had the conflicts with the shopkeeper?" VZ: "Yes." PC: "Okay. And Mr. Popadic was there all the time throughout those discussions?" VZ: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I saw you, you but I wanted to wait until this was concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I didn't want to disturb. Some portions of this transcript does not represent all of the record, as far as we know it, in B/C/S and also in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if it does so in any material particular, you can bring it to our attention. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would also note -- well, for the record, let me just ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is that -- is that an accurate recording of what you said during the interview with Phil Caine?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that Mr. Popadic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking for a fuller explanation. Mr. Cepic can ask you that. I'm just asking, what you heard here on tape, did you recognize your voice? Were those your words that we heard on the tape?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognized my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender T001-1686, clip 2, into evidence, recognising that maybe over the course of today I will work with Mr. Cepic to resolve whatever he sees as an inaccuracy, and hopefully we can resolve that. If not, then I would ask that the tape be submitted to CLSS, and I will be bound by their determination of what is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to continue where my learned friend stopped, I propose that this exhibit would be marked for identification until we clarify situation related to those mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour. I'd agree with that with respect to the translation, but the witness has said, Those are my words, and it's really his words that are really what's important. The translation is something that can be corrected, but I'd hate to let this witness leave without having resolved that this is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the witness did say that those were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not object that the witness gave interview. We do not object that those words are his words, but the problem is in translation. As Mr. Groome said, we had very bad translation in Belgrade during that interview, so that's the problem, and a couple times we changed a couple -- we tried to solve that situation. And finally on the first day, we received additional translation, actually, the new translation of that interview, and during the week, we checked that and found quite a number of mistakes, and yesterday afternoon we sent to OTP all those mistakes which we found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, you wish to wade in?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just because I was following the -- it appears the English is not even correct, so it's not a matter of translation. It's just a matter of a bad transcript, so I think we should probably resubmit it or somehow get a transcript, because as it stands now, we don't have a translation of the man's words into a language that non-B/C/S speakers can appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I might be able to shorten this. I will agree that only the tape is introduced at this stage, and I will work over the next few days to have a transcript that is agreeable or is agreed by all the parties as an accurate transcript of the tape. But it seems to me that voice, that the recording itself has been authenticated. That really must come into evidence. It's really a question about translation, and I will agree to undertake, to work with my colleagues to ensure that everyone agrees that the translation is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then that can be admitted separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, then. So we'll admit the tape and the translation will be considered for admission at a later date after it has been verified.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will become Exhibit P204.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivkovic. I have no further questions. Your Honour, there is some confusions about exhibits but perhaps we could wait until the end of the examination, and then we can clarify that then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivkovic, here I go again. First of all, have you ever actually served a prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Compared to you, what age is Mr. Sredoje Lukic? Younger? Older?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately my age. I don't know his exact year of birth, but he's approximately my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, this shop, was it the only one or were there other shops in the village?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was the only shop in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivkovic, do you remember the year 1992 for other things except the breakout of the war?

utterances.speaker: VEROLJUB ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it by the inflation, the beginning of the war. In my memory, those are the darkest years of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one matter that's unresolved. Perhaps we might deal with it now. It has to do with the table prepared by the Prosecution of the information provided by the government of Serbia. It's ZIVK-CONV. According to the registrar, there hasn't been a ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought we had admitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was my memory, as well, Your Honour, but I think perhaps that matter needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admitted it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, just to clarify, I think there seems to be some confusion, I think perhaps in part caused by me when I misquoted an ERN number, but the first instance judgement is ERN 0645-2787, 0645-2801. I believe that was admitted as P199. And then the second instance judgement was 0645-2807, 0645-2809, and I believe that was admitted as P201. I just wanted to clarify that was in fact accorded with the Chamber's and the registrar's recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, two matters. First thing, I hope that we will receive from Mr. Groome the document which he mentioned in his examination relating to the attempt of deleting of judgement, so I would be very grateful if OTP provides me with that document. And for the second issue, before we have witness in the courtroom, I kindly ask for a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lukic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your full first and family name.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Zorka Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please state the date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: The 7th of October, 1966, in Prijepolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exhibit number -- 65 ter exhibit number 26. ID number of this document is in B/C/S 2D05-0130, and in English, 2D05-0276, in accordance with the Defence notification from 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lukic, did you speak to Prosecution investigations on the 4th of June, 2008, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the screen. Madam, did you -- 28th of November, during your proofing session with lawyers of the Defence of Mr. Sredoje Lukic, after being shown a transcript, you explained the statements -- statements on page 2, 16th and 17th line, and on page 3, 5 and 6 -- lines 5 and 6, words, Sredoje remembered exactly the date when I gave birth and that he visit me the next day and he informed the lawyers. What did you want to make more precise in relation to this transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that Sredoje Lukic visited me with his family on the 27th of June, 1992, the following day that I had emerged from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Lukic, if I were to ask you the same questions today that you were asked by the Prosecution investigator during that interview, would you provide the same answers that you provided on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam Lukic, why would June 1992, be significant to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: It is very significant to me because on the 22nd of June, 1992, my second child was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system, ID number is 2D04-0186, and in English is 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at the screen, and please explain what this document we see means.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a birth certificate of my child, which states the date of birth, the place of birth of my -- and the name of my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is not in the record. I kindly ask for admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have document, ID number is 2D03-0264, in English is 65. If we have technical problems, I can provide a hard copy. We cannot see on our screens. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: This document states the date when I was discharged from hospital, when I went out of the hospital with my baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you state the date.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: 26th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see copy in English language, which is also attached to B/C/S version on ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Both documents are in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I kindly ask admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just inquire, is the original of this document being tendered, or is it simply a scanned of the original? Just want to know exactly what is being tendered. It's a very, very important document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OTP had opportunity to check this document, and Mr. Cole visited my assistant in the Defence room to check the authenticity of this document, a couple of months ago during the OTP phase, and they checked that. So we admit this document, and original is available in any moment, if you need to check something, just call us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that the -- given the critical nature of this, I would ask that the original of this document be what's tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is not possible, Your Honour. Technically, technically it is not possible to be in e-court system original sheet. As I said, Mr. Cole gave me a call, he checked the document, and he didn't ask anything additional about that document. It was a couple months ago. I also kept that e-mail, and the 13th of November was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And the 13th of November was the deadline for the checking of documents. We fully complied with the rules and also with this document, so we ask admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Groome, if the document is admissible in accordance with our rules, why are you asking for the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, I think the best evidence rule would really be applicable here because if you look at the image, Your Honour, you can see a faint line running down from about the middle of the top, down across the right-hand corner, and coming out on the bottom. The critical information on this document has been torn. The document, as far as I understand it, and please, Mr. Cepic, correct me if I'm wrong, but the critical information on this document was actually torn. The document is a torn document. I believe for the Chamber to assess its reliability, the Chamber should have the benefit of seeing the original document itself and not have to rely on simply a photocopy of the document. If it's available, I mean, I submit that this should be marked for identification, and I certainly won't object to Mr. Cepic seeking to replace that document at a later stage with the original as soon as he can bring it to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where do you say the critical information is that is torn on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at the fourth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you look at the fourth line down, the critical piece of information for this document is 26.6.92, the day that Ms. Lukic says that she was discharged from the hospital, that being the day before Sredoje Lukic came to visit, and now with it enlarged, you can see the tear along the document and how that portion of the document is actually torn from the remainder of the document. So I would submit the Chamber, in order to properly assess the reliability of this document, should have the original before it so it can examine the torn document and make its own assessment about its reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, is it possible to produce a clearer scan of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My assistant will try to do their best in that way, but I also, for the record, have to add a line one more time. OTP had the opportunity of a couple months to check this document. Mr. Cole checked the original document in the Defence room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that doesn't prevent -- that doesn't prevent any party from raising an objection in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Of course. And they had opportunity, of course, to check in a hospital or somewhere else that -- the authenticity of this document, from who it's issued and the dates and other necessary things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the record is clear, we did attempt that, and all records were destroyed. They're destroyed after a period of ten years, so again, this is the only remaining copy of this document. The original is available. It seems prudent that it should be produced before the Court so the Court can assess it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the original available?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my possession is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On the first break -- on the first break, I need 20 minutes to reach my office and to bring it back to the courtroom, so just if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We would like to see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we'll admit this one, but we'll see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 2D46, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam Lukic, just one question. You explained quite a lot of things in the interview with the Prosecutor, and you stated at one point that Sredoje Lukic had done everything he could to leave Visegrad and to settle in Serbia. Was his intention to do so temporarily, for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Sredoje's intentions were to leave Visegrad indefinitely because in Visegrad the war had started, the living conditions were inadequate, the children couldn't go to school, there was a shortage of food together with all the other dire circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Lukic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Lukic. My name is Dermot Groome, and I'll be asking you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution. I'd first like to begin by asking you, can you tell us, your last name is Lukic. How precisely are you related to Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: My family name is Lukic. That's correct. Sredoje is my husband's brother, so he's my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Slavko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What other siblings are there aside from Sredoje Lukic and Slavko Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: They have another brother, Rade Lukic, and two sisters, Vojka and Savka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it true that prior to the war, you would make the trip to Visegrad to visit Sredoje Lukic and his family at his family home? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to your interview, you did that approximately two ore three times a year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the name of the neighborhood that he lived in Visegrad is Seganje, S-e-g-a-n-j-e, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Seganje, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He was a policeman in Visegrad, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on the occasions that you went to see him there, did it appear that he was well-liked by his neighbors and the people of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: He was liked. They liked him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you get the sense that he was well known in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Since he was working as a policeman, it's most probable that he was well known. Yes, he was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What would you estimate his height to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: What would I estimate his height? Well, he's as tall as my husband. He's tall, strapping, 1 metre and 80 centimetres, approximately. I never really paid that much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would you say he weighed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: What he weighed in 1992? I can tell you approximately between 80 and 90 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how did he wear his hair in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Short, cropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you work outside the home?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you mean? I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to being the mother of your children and taking care of the household, did you ever engage in any other work outside the home?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was on maternity leave during that period. After maternity leave, I went back to employment. I was employed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was your employment?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you ask me where I work?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm more interested, in 1992, are you working at the same place --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not work. I was on maternity leave. I was at home with the baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you work prior to going on maternity leave?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I worked in Lipov Lad in the Boulevard of Revolution. First I was on sick leave during my pregnancy and then went on maternity leave after giving birth. This means I was missing from work for one month -- one year and six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do? I'm trying to get at what type of work did you engage in?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I work in the catering and hospitality industry. That's my trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the birth of your child in 1992. What is the child's name?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragana Lukic. That's the name of my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I imagine that you and your husband took photographs as all proud parents do at the time of a birth, and you'd be able to produce them to the Court if required?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not bring any photos, but if necessary, I can supply at a later date. I can give it -- give them to the lawyer, but I don't have them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it your evidence that Sredoje Lukic came to visit you the day after you arrived home after giving birth to your child in June of 1992? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic visited on the 27th of June, and I was discharged from hospital on the 26th of June. So the following day from my discharge from hospital, Sredoje and his family visited me at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what time that day did they arrive at your home?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Around mid-day, noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Some four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd also imagine that in the four hours that they were there, pictures were also taken of Sredoje Lukic holding his new niece. Would you be able to provide us with photographs taken on the 27th showing Sredoje Lukic holding this newborn?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not take any photographs. We did not have a camera at the time, so we did not take any pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you do not have a picture of Sredoje Lukic holding the baby shortly after birth on the 27th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have such a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: According to your account, both your husband Slavko Lukic and Sredoje's wife Vidjenka Lukic were present during this visit and could also speak to it. Do you know why your husband is not coming to testify about this event?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After which visit, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This question is calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask her, Your Honour, if she knows why her husband -- I mean, presumably they discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's a proper question for her at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You know that Sredoje Lukic was held by some Muslims -- held in captivity in Visegrad, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Given that I had a small child and was pregnant with another, of course I heard and I saw on TV that he had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you said in your interview that he visited you and your family shortly after his release when he was looking for a job in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your interview, you said to the investigator that shortly after he was released from captivity, he came to Belgrade to look for a job and that he visited with you and your family. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: He visited me after I had been discharged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we have the reference for this question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's page 6, beginning at line 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, I'm talking about before you had the baby but after the period between the time Sredoje Lukic was released from captivity in Visegrad but prior to when you had Dragana. Did Sredoje Lukic come and visit you during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I think he did once. I don't remember the exact date or time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the purpose of coming to Belgrade was he was looking to get a job in Belgrade with the police. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, he was trying to leave Visegrad, of course. I told you earlier he was looking for a way to leave Visegrad because of the situation that prevailed there and because of his children. He couldn't keep his children in school there. He couldn't put any food on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But his intention was to attempt to get a job through a relative who was working in the police in Belgrade. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was trying through a relative of theirs whose name is Sreten Lukic who was already working in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this person, Sreten Lukic, had a high-ranking position in the Ministry of the Interior. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is the same Sreten Lukic that is currently in custody here in The Hague. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Sredoje Lukic after he had been released from captivity, did he describe the treatment that he was subjected to?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No, he did not discuss these things with me or before me or before my children and certainly not before his own children. He talked to my husband, though, and I don't know what exactly they talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any of the injuries he sustained when he was held in captivity?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't show me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding that after Sredoje Lukic was released from captivity, he returned to work as a police officer in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He returned to work there as a policeman in Visegrad. His family was away. He went back to Visegrad to work, but he regularly visited with his family in Belgrade, and in the meantime he was looking for a job as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, also according to your interview, you also know Milan Lukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in fact, he attended your wedding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What would you say his height is?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: His may be a little less tall than Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would you say his weight was back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's been no foundation that she saw him in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, does --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can answer. He was a bit thinner, maybe 75 to 80 kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saying all this roughly because I didn't weigh them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you didn't weigh him. It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We break for half an hour. Just before the break, Mr. Cepic, you had undertaken to fetch the original of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And half an hour will be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, half an hour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, we were talking about Milan Lukic just when we took the break. The last question I have from -- with respect to Milan Lukic is that during the month of June 1992, you don't ever recall seeing him in Belgrade, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, foundation, speculation. This is not proper testimony for this witness. It's not raised in direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it is a proper question. She's a relative of his. I'm just asking a simple question of whether she saw him in the month of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have read in your interview how you described becoming involved as a witness in this case. Can I conclude that your husband first spoke to you about this, or maybe -- can you tell us how you first became involved as a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Lawyer Cepic contacted me sometime around the new year, and Sredoje remembered the date when I gave birth and that the day after I left the hospital, he visited me. He told that to his lawyer, and that's how I established contact with his lawyer. However, since I was unable to find the letter of discharge - I had misplaced it - I couldn't remember whether it was the 25th or the 26th of June when I left the hospital. I found the letter of discharge later, and my husband gave it to the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with your husband the possibility of testifying on behalf of his brother?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So prior to Mr. Cepic contacting you, you had no idea about the important testimony that you might be able to provide?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I did not think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as you've stated here, it was Sredoje Lukic who remembered the exact date of the birth of Dragana, not you remembering that Sredoje was accused of a crime in proximity to the birth of Dragana. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a little confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognize that, Your Honour. Let me break it up. I apologize.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologize for giving you such a confusing question. Let me try to break it down. As you've said here, it was Sredoje who first realized that -- or remembered the exact date that Dragana was born?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your best recollection of when Mr. Cepic contacted you and told him -- and you told him that Sredoje was visiting you shortly after the birth of your child was around last new year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: It was towards the end of 2007, the beginning of 2008, around the new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Are the -- is the -- are the earphones okay? You seem to be maybe having -- experiencing some discomfort when I speak. Are they too loud? We can get you some assistance with that.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after the new year, on 8th of January, 2008, to be precise, Mr. Cepic filed what is referred to here as alibi notice where he is required to provide information about where Sredoje Lukic says that he was and the witnesses who will testify on his behalf. In that filing, after the time you said you spoke with Mr. Cepic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I see Mr. Cepic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does Mr. Groome raise his final arguments or what. This witness is not able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is inaudible. Terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you're not being heard. You have to speak into the mic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I think that Mr. Groome now did not raise his final arguments because I think that this witness cannot provide us information related to the Defence motions or similar issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We haven't yet heard the question. What is the question, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I won't repeat the whole explanation, but on the 8th [Realtime transcript read in error "28th"] of January, 2008, when Mr. Cepic, as required by the rules, provided the names of the people who would be able to testify about Sredoje Lukic's whereabouts during the time he was alleged to have committed the crime, you were not put forward as a witness. You were only put forward as a witness in June of 2008. Does that change your recollection as to when you spoke to Mr. Cepic about this evidence that you had?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I told you that I was unable to find the letter of discharge immediately, so I told Mr. Cepic that until I find the letter of discharge I cannot be sure. I found the letter of discharge only in April. I had mislaid it in some books where you normally don't keep documents, but that's where I put it, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the indictment against Sredoje Lukic was made public in October of the year 2000, and he was a fugitive for about five years until he turned himself in in September of 2005. Did you see him during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know if your husband was in communication with him during that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know where he was staying during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But when the case was made public against him, you recognized that Sredoje Lukic, the relative of yours, was -- had been indicted for some serious crimes committed in Visegrad in June of 1992, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once the indictment became public and there were public arrest warrants issued for Sredoje Lukic, it was publicized in the media, you recognized that the Sredoje Lukic who had been indicted was the Sredoje Lukic who was your husband's brother. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course he's my husband's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you were aware once the indictment became public that your husband's brother was wanted, was a fugitive, with respect to some serious crimes that occurred in Visegrad in June of 1992, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew he was on the run, but I didn't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you and your husband ever discuss the crimes with which Sredoje Lukic had been charged?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any crimes that he may have committed. I didn't see that, so I couldn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But there was substantial media coverage about this case and about the crimes underlying this case. Were you not exposed to any of that media coverage during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I did listen to all the talk that was going on, and there was a lot of talk, but I didn't see anything for myself and therefore couldn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it never occur to you prior to Mr. Cepic calling that the two most serious acts that Sredoje was charged with occurred in the same month as the birth of your own daughter? Did that never occur to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't even know when these acts were committed. I never gave it any thought. All I know is that he visited the day after my second child was born, and when these crimes were committed, I don't know. I was not interested. You have to believe that I don't even know what happened on that 27th. All I know is that he called on me. He came with his wife and his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, is it your testimony that you had no interest in the fact that your husband's brother had been indicted by an international criminal tribunal for serious crimes? Is that your evidence, that you had no interest in that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know in which way you mean it, I had no interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just want to intervene. In transcript, page 84, line 3, "All I know is that he called on me." But witness said [B/C/S spoken]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which is what?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said, Mr. Cepic quotes, "He was at my place." Interpreter's note, it's -- Mr. Cepic misunderstands the meaning of the expression "call on someone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's virtually the same thing in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "He was at my place" is virtually the same thing as "he called on me," in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, at page 83, line 25, the record records you as saying, "I was not interested." My question to you is, is that really a true statement, that you had no interest in the fact that your husband's brother had been indicted for serious crimes by an international criminal tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: You know what? It's not that I had no interest. Of course I had some interest, but I had one very small child, and I was pregnant with another, and after that I had a third child, and I was so busy with my children that I had no time to deal with other things, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you and your husband ever, over the dinner table or after the children had gone to bed, ever discuss that his brother had been charged by an international tribunal and there was an outstanding arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in those discussions, did it never -- was it never discussed what the substance of the allegations were against Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I heard he was indicted and charged with certain crimes, but again, I had not that much interest in it, not enough to go into things like whether it was on that date or on a different date. I had too many of my problems to go into the details of what he's supposed to have done or if he had done it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, I appreciate that you may be in a difficult position, but I put it to you that the reason that you never came forward with this information prior to just a year ago is the same reason that you do not have a photograph of Sredoje Lukic holding his newborn niece, and that is that while you may have been discharged from the hospital on the 26th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had an assertion here, and we don't know what this assertion is corroborated by.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What assertion are you talking about? He's putting his case as he's obliged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but it sounds a little bit different to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's his case on his instructions, and he's quite rightly putting it, and I just wish more lawyers would do that. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just recap my question to you. So I'm putting to you that the reason that you had not come forward in the seven years since the indictment was made public with this very, very important information that could exonerate him is the very same reason that you do not have a photograph of him during his four-hour visit with your newborn niece, and that is because, although it may be true that you were discharged from the hospital on the 26th, I put it to you that it is not true that he visited you on the 27th, the precise day he is alleged to have been in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I maintain to you that he visited me on the 27th of June, 1992, the day after I left the hospital with my newborn. He visited me together with his wife and his children. I did not have a camera at the time to be able to take a photo, and he didn't have one either. I had a picture of my baby taken only at the hospital as we were leaving. There is a picture of the baby alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just tell us, who are the other persons who were there during that visit by Sredoje? Can you just list all of them for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband; myself; my elder daughter, a baby; Sredoje; his wife; and his children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anybody from outside the family? Was there anybody there not a member of family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, is there any possibility in your mind that it may have been a different day shortly after the birth of the baby, perhaps the 28th, the 29th, the 30th? Is there any possibility that that could be true given the fact that it's so many years in the past now?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a very important date to me. I remember all the first visits that I received after the birth of my first, my second, and the third baby. The birthdays of my children are very important to me, and also important to me are the people who came to visit me immediately after I left the hospital, the maternity ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What gift did Sredoje bring?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: The custom in our parts is to give a gift of money, and that's what he gave us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if I were to ask you for each of your children all of the people who visited -- visited you, the first time they visited, you are confident that you would be able to give an accurate and reliable list of those people and the dates on which they visited -- visited you after giving birth to a child?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. After the birth of my first child, my mother and brother were the first to visit as soon as I came home. After my second child, it was Sredoje with his wife and children. After my third child, unfortunately, no one came within the first month because Belgrade was being bombed at the time and nobody was able to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why are you able to recollect Sredoje's visit as taking place on the day after you came out of the hospital as distinct from, say, two or three days after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I always remember these things, the first people who call on me, and he came the day after, immediately after I came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, I just want to conclude by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, are you calling any of the other family members who were present during Sredoje's visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- we announced the list just of four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's -- you don't intend to call her husband or the children, any of the children?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We thought that would be sufficient for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a correction to the transcript. On page 81, line 7, it's been made known to me that it should say 8th of January, 2008, not 28th of January, so I'd ask that that correction be made to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, could you tell us the dates of birth of Sredoje Lukic's two children?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. I know that his son is older than my eldest daughter. Danijela [phoen] was born in 1988, and my daughter was born in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- just intervene in transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Cepic come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line 14, it is not Danijela but Danila [phoen], the name of the child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Danila.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to read you a brief transcript of your interview, which is now in evidence, and the reference is page 2, lines 2 to 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAINE ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "How did he contact you?" And the "he" refers to Mr. Cepic. And you responded: "Well, Sredoje remembered the exact date when I gave birth and that he visited me the next day, so he has informed the attorney to contact me, and that is how we got in touch ." It remains a fact that you did not come up -- that you did not realize that the date that Sredoje Lukic came to visit you was important. It was something that was told to you actually quite recently. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has been given the original document with the discharge. Have you seen it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I took a quick look at the break, Your Honour. I do plan to take a closer look, perhaps, but I have no objection now to that document being introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit the original of the document. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original will be admitted and kept in the vault, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Here it is. Mr. Cepic [microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for his Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to testify. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your mic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the indictment in counts 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17 recites on or about 27th June, et cetera, et cetera. And is it your case that this event took place on the 27th or on or about the 27th?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as stated in the indictment, it is on or about. As the Chamber will recall during the course of the Prosecution case, some witnesses had slightly different recollections as to the precise date, so that is why it is pled in that way. That is pled with as much specificity as possible, again, to take into account the variation, the slight variation of the date between the different witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll, of course, be checking into that. I thought most of the witnesses did testify fairly specifically to the 27th, but that is something which we'll obviously be checking. The next witness. No, before you call the witness, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not happy with the explanation that has been offered by the Defence for the unavailability of the two witnesses. You said that was disclosed to you just recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. Friday evening is when I talked with the one witness. I have not heard back from the second witness, Mr. -- I don't know if their -- the filing was confidential, but I think I can testify that it was the one -- the first witness is the one that I had spoke with on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a good start, Mr. Ivetic, because you have to do your best. I know it may be difficult, but you have to have your witnesses. I will be fairly flexible, but I don't expect a Defence case to be presented on the basis where we are going to have a witness on a Monday, then the case breaks down because that witness's testimony is finished, and there is no other witness available. So I really have to express the hope that this is going to be the exception, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope so, as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what is the nature of the other engagement that makes it impossible for this witness to attend?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was it not -- why wasn't that known from the time the witness was asked to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As Your Honour may recall, when we filed the 65 ter statements and then we received -- we received the notice that we were going to redo the statements, we only had two witnesses that we could call that we for sure were going to keep on the list, which are the two witness that we identified in our weekly notification. The witnesses had previously scheduled professional obligations. This one that I talked with had the professional obligation that kept him unable to travel this week. I'm hopeful that we can schedule him perhaps for next week or by that time we'll have the revised list with the final list of witnesses so we can try to get someone else over here. With respect to the second witness, I haven't heard back from him, so I can't confirm him, and I believe the notification that we filed said that we had not yet had an opportunity to confirm those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... testimony with these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The notification that we filed said that we have not yet had an opportunity to confirm the appearance of those two witnesses for this week. The notification notice was filed on Thursday of last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the question is why? You say it's now likely that we are going to have a breakdown. The pace at which your colleague is progressing, it's quite quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and had we not had the last week with me engaged in the other matter, perhaps I could have gone to terrain and gotten some more witnesses. All these things have an effect on the Defence case, Your Honour. All these things have an effect on the work that we have to do, and as counsel we have obligations to take care of everything that comes up, and especially when something comes up on an emergent basis as it did last week, that is something that affected our ability to do more than we did to prepare for the beginning of our Defence case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you explain to me what the nature of the other obligation is? I can't remember. I just asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We had -- the other obligation, Your Honour, was we had the Prosecution file a request under Rule 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I meant the other obligation which makes it not possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Previously scheduled professional obligation for Mr. Rasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but what is the nature of that professional obligation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting to get the written confirmation from him but I thought I'd bring it to Your Honours' attention as soon as possible precisely because of the fact that it involves scheduling for this week which is why I raised it today rather than waiting to get the confirmation from him. But when I spoke to him on the phone he mentioned that he could not travel this week because of the previously scheduled obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That sounds very vague. You must have that explanation by tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to give the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to go back to the prior issue about the date, one of the ways where it is not clear is Vidovdan Day is, according to the calendar that's in -- before the Chamber now, is on the 28th, and some witnesses talked about the event happening on Vidovdan Day. Although I'm not clear whether it was the night into the morning of Vidovdan or Vidovdan Day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, could we start tomorrow morning? We did not expect that we would be quite fast. We expected that we would spend more time in preliminary issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. In the circumstances, I think yes. We'll adjourn and resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of December, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.25 p.m.,
